implementation_notes: A Java interface declares public abstract methods (and constants, implicitly public static final) and cannot hold instance state - the stateless part is compiler-enforced, which makes this the pattern in its purest form. Since Java 8 a contract member may carry a body, so a published interface can grow without breaking implementors, and static methods host factories and helpers next to the contract; a single-abstract-method interface additionally converts from a lambda, which is how a contract becomes a strategy at the call site. The only thing an interface cannot supply is shared state, so use an abstract class when the contract genuinely needs fields or a constructor, and treat the interface as the default.
pitfalls: Adding an abstract method to a published interface breaks every implementor at compile time; a default method avoids that but can only build on the interface's own API.

Default methods collide when a class implements two interfaces declaring the same signature - the class must override and resolve explicitly (A.super.m()), so diamond rules reappear in the contract layer.
Constant interfaces: members are implicitly public static final and stay in the API forever, which is why an interface used as a constants bag is an anti-pattern.
Interfaces with primitive parameters force boxing when implementations are lambdas or generic code; a hot contract may serve better as an abstract class or a generic type parameter.

variants.name: Sealed interface (closed contract)
variants.idiom_name: sealed interface with permits + pattern-matching switch
variants.implementation_notes: A sealed interface with a permits clause restricts implementation to the named types, so the contract becomes a closed, known set of variants and a pattern-matching switch over it can be checked for exhaustiveness. Choose it when the role is deliberately closed - an expression tree, a result type, a protocol message set - and every consumer should handle all cases; keep an unsealed interface when new implementations should appear without editing the contract. This is the point where the interface turns from an open substitutability seam into a sum type, and the declaration states which of the two it is.
pitfalls: Permitted subtypes must live in the same module (and package for the unnamed module), so a sealed contract cannot be implemented by downstream consumers at all - the decision is not reversible without breaking them.
Exhaustiveness is checked only where the switch is total over the sealed hierarchy; adding a variant later turns every such switch into a source-incompatible change.
Sealing does not make implementations immutable: a permitted class can still hold mutable state, and records are only shallowly immutable.
